selected : sin(th*2.0004673)
relative RMS error : 0.0100

The table is the hall of fame: one row per complexity, with the loss of the best expression found at that complexity and the expression itself, already simplified. Read it as the Pareto front of size against error, the symbolic-regression version of the number-of-terms curve of Sparse Regression for Equation Discovery. The loss falls as the complexity rises until $\sin 2\theta$ appears, and past that point the extra nodes buy nothing, so the front has its elbow at the law. The row PySR selects by default is chosen by a score that rewards a large drop in loss for a small increase in complexity, which is the elbow rule made automatic, and the selected expression is returned in sympy form with its constants already optimized. The full law follows by multiplying back, $R = (v^2/g)\sin 2\theta$. Nothing about the search changed between the failure and the success; the problem was made one a search could solve.

Remark (what to carry over). Everything this notebook did by hand is in PySR: the population and the operators of Chapter 3, the trees of Chapter 4, the parsimony of Chapter 5, and the refinement of constants. What PySR cannot do is the work before the search: choosing the variables, reducing them by dimensional analysis, and deciding what counts as simple. That remains the scientist's part, with any engine.




7. Where Discovery Stands¶

Three notebooks have presented three methods, and they are best seen as one method with increasing freedom and increasing cost.


Sparse regression SINDy Symbolic regression
Finds coefficients of given terms coefficients of given terms, per equation the expression itself
Needs a library a library and derivatives of the data operators, variables, and patience
Cost milliseconds seconds minutes to hours
Deterministic yes yes no
Fails when the law is not in the library, or the library is collinear the derivative is too noisy, or the library is wrong the search space is too large, or constants are needed
Best for algebraic laws with known candidate forms dynamics with polynomial or otherwise listable right-hand sides laws of unknown form in few variables

The practical order is this. Reduce the problem first, by dimensional analysis, since every method benefits and symbolic regression depends on it. Try a library, because if the law is in it the answer is immediate and exact, and the Pareto curve will say whether it is. If the curve has no elbow, run a free search, and read its result as a proposal for the library rather than as a final law. Refine constants by least squares, validate by extrapolation, and repeat with different seeds and thresholds until the answer stops changing.


The tools keep improving. PySR, used in Section 6.3, is the most capable symbolic-regression engine available at the time of writing and handles problems of ten or more variables; the methods it implements are the ones this notebook built by hand, and a reader who has followed the hand-built engine will find nothing in it that is new in kind.




Summary¶

Key takeaways

  • A library-based method finds only what the library contains; $\sin(x^2)$ defeated an eight-term polynomial library at every threshold, and a library large enough to contain everything is too collinear to use.
  • Searching expressions is a search without gradients. Local search stops on the first hill it climbs; a heuristic gives up the guarantee of optimality to search such spaces anyway, simulated annealing by accepting downhill moves with a decaying probability, the genetic algorithm by keeping a population.
  • A genetic algorithm has four parts: an encoding of solutions as chromosomes, a non-negative fitness to be maximized, selection with probability increasing in fitness, and the two operators crossover, which recombines two parents, and mutation, which injects what the population lacks. A population learns where the landscape is good, which a single point cannot.
  • Symbolic regression searches expressions directly. An expression is a tree; genetic programming is the same loop with subtree crossover and mutation and tournament selection, scored by error plus a parsimony penalty, with linear scaling so that the search finds shapes and least squares finds amplitudes.
  • Dimensional analysis decides whether a search succeeds. The projectile was unsolvable on its raw variables and solved at once on its dimensionless group.

Looking ahead. Discovery closes a loop that the rest of this course opened. Physics-Informed Neural Networks put a known equation into the training of a network; Deep Neural Operators and Fourier Neural Operator learned the solution map of a known equation from data. The three discovery notebooks ask where the equation comes from when it is not known, and answer that it can come from the data, provided that what is known, the units, the symmetries, the candidate forms, is given to the method first. Equations found this way can be handed back to a PINN as its physics, and that is the direction in which the field is moving: networks that fit data, discover the equation that the fit obeys, and are then constrained by the equation they discovered.
